extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, rhetoric, and 19th-century oratory
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and character-sketch standards for judging public speaking, conversational manner, and written style as exemplified by early-19th-century critics (sketches of Jeffrey, Brougham, Burdett). Useful for evaluating or composing speeches, critiques, and character portraits of orators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range_of_knowledge_and_familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Has a great range of knowledge, an equal familiarity with the principles and the details of a subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valued quality: broad and deep information enables apt illustration and authoritative argument. Anti-pattern: knowledge so excessive that it encumbers or stifles originality (see 'excess of knowledge' in Scottish eloquence). Example: Jeffrey's strength consists in great range of knowledge and apt illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural_acuteness_and_discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural acuteness and discrimination of the logician with habitual caution and coolness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides measured, well-reasoned responses and the ability to qualify extravagant theories by practical objections or speculative doubts. Recommended for editors/critics to avoid dogmatism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension_of_judgment_and_well-balanced_moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspension of judgment and well-balanced moderation of sentiments resulting from discursiveness of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive view of all circumstances often yields common-place conclusions; moderation prevents being duped by prejudice or enthusiasm. Anti-pattern: excessive suspension that becomes indecision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapidity_variety_and_aptness_of_illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Brilliancy of manner often resolves into the rapidity, variety and aptness of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent, varied examples keep writing lively and prevent dullness; caution that over-reliance on illustration can mask deeper originality or substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facility_of_transitions_and_vivacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Number, liveliness and facility of transitions keep up an appearance of vivacity and novel, sparkling effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good for sustaining reader/audience interest; anti-pattern: excessive transitions can be a sign of discursiveness that avoids sustained focus on a central point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy_vs_copiousness_of_language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language may be more copious than select; sometimes two or three words perform the office of one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copiousness is advantageous in extempore speaking (prevents dead stops), but in written composition it can give an air of carelessness or over-labour. Aim for selectness in writing; allow copiousness in speech where rhythm and flow matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-speaking_style_translated_to_writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of a person accustomed to public speaking: no pause, flow, redundance and volubility like a stream or rolling-stone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-speaking habits (fluency, rapidity) produce neatness and epigrammatic point, but when applied to writing can lead to agreeable diffuseness or an appearance of undue ease; writers should moderate spoken manner in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_flowery_or_affected_expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Not a flowery or affected writer; few tropes, figures, or odd startling thoughts in expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer ingenuity and pertinent examples over ornament. Excessive ornamentation (flowery style) is an anti-pattern; clarity and pertinence preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational_liveliness_and_variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversation equally lively, various, and instructive; ready to take up any subject without preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conversationally versatile speaker can enliven public discourse; anti-pattern: inability to be silent or to listen—listening should weigh impressions rather than only prepare replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency_to_cross-examine_and_argumentative_habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Bound to dispute and answer as if in Court; listens not to judge but to reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While rhetorical disputation displays acuteness, it is a fault in private or intimate contexts; speakers should avoid automatic cross-examination that ignores others' impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profuseness_of_encomiums_with_reservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Profuse in encomiums and admiration of others, but with reservation of a right to differ or to blame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity of praise balanced by independent judgement is an admirable social and critical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impetus_vs_mechanism_in_oratory (Irish_vs_Scottish_contrast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Irish eloquence: offspring of impulse, full of fancy; Scotch eloquence: offspring of mechanism, weighed down with facts and logical deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation: impulse/fancy brings life and originality (even if extravagant) and may be disciplined; mechanism/excessive reliance on formality and learned models can render oratory lifeless and unoriginal. Favor balance—discipline fancy rather than overlearned formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_fancy_alliteration_antithesis_and_metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Irish oratory uses whim and fancy, alliteration and antithesis, heated passion and bloated metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices give fire and imagination; anti-pattern: unlettered neglect of subject and natural confusion of ideas. Use rhetorical figures with purpose; avoid empty pageantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess_of_knowledge_as_an_obstacle_to_imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess of knowledge encumbers eloquence: a load of topics and forms of logic precludes originality or beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t let learning bury imagination; avoid turning living bursts of passion into dead commonplaces through over-reliance on authorities and learned models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_life_and_motion_over_negative_formality
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle of life and motion is the primary condition of genius; the luxuriant wildness may be disciplined, the dry and rigid formality cannot burst its shell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing oratory, prioritize vivacity and imaginative force; rigid correctness alone is insufficient to move audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance_between_abstract_principles_and_immediate_facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Some speakers deal less in abstract principles and more in individual, immediate facts (Brougham); others in general topics and balance of argument (Mackintosh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches have merit; use facts to ground arguments but avoid so many details that the spirit or point is lost. Tailor the mix to audience and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy_of_presentation_and_focusing_on_point
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid moving in an unmanageable procession of facts; premises should not overlay and block up the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to bring the audience to the conclusion without overloading with antecedent detail. Anti-pattern: so many particulars that the main point is obscured or the conclusion arrives too late.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience_patience_and_reserve_of_discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely excessively on the patience of hearers or discard reserve and discretion—going to the full length of the tether often overshoots the mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of listeners’ limits; holding back some material and deploying it judiciously often serves a cause better than continuous unrestrained outpouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need_for_co-operation_and_consideration_of_colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader must consult and co-operate; excessive independence or improvisatory turns can leave colleagues and allies in the lurch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political or public leaders should temper adventurousness with co-operation; rhetorical heroics that disregard partners are strategic faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate_scale_of_subject_and_style
rubrics_metrics.description: Some speakers 'must have a pretty large question to discuss'—are heavy in style and unsuited to petty occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match rhetorical weight and stylistic density to the scale of the occasion. Anti-pattern: applying 'weighty' modes to trivial subjects wastes force and bores audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainness_honesty_and_common_sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain, unaffected delivery, common sense and common honesty command popular attention and favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courageous plain-speaking, without vanity or duplicity, is effective and wins public trust; avoid unnecessary ornament when sincerity and clarity suffice (example: Sir Francis Burdett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation_and_mellowed_principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles mellowed and improved with time without becoming less sound; not violent except in extreme occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enduring rhetorical authority comes from consistent, tempered principles—excessive vehemence is only justified when situation demands; otherwise moderation is preferable.
